summary: Extends the Remote Network Monitoring MIB with objects for watching IEEE 802.5 Token Ring networks. It was a standards-track specification. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A Token Ring is a circle where a token gets passed around so only the holder can talk. This memo adds gauges so a monitor can watch such a circle.

questions: how to monitor token ring with snmp
what are token ring isolating errors
what is the rmon token ring mib
subtitle: Remote monitoring objects for 802.5 Token Ring networks, extending the RMON MIB.

tldr.problem: The Remote Network Monitoring MIB defined its media-specific statistics and history objects only for Ethernet, so Token Ring LANs could not be monitored by a probe in the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines Token Ring versions of the statistics and history groups, plus four Token Ring only groups: Ring Station, Ring Station Order, Ring Station Config and Source Routing Statistics. All hang under tokenRing { rmon 10 }.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 1271. All the groups are optional to implement. The RFC is now Historic.

today: RFC 1513 is Historic, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. It updates RFC 1271.

sections.title: Why a Token Ring Extension
sections.content:
RFC 1271 defines a framework for remote monitoring on a network probe, with objects broken into nine functional groups. Two of those groups, statistics and history, depend on the media type, and RFC 1271 defined the media-specific objects only for Ethernet. This memo does the same for Token Ring LANs.

It sits in the Internet-standard Network Management Framework: the SMI (RFC 1155 and RFC 1212), MIB-II (RFC 1213) and SNMP (RFC 1157).
sections.plainLanguage: A monitoring tool already knew how to watch one kind of network. This memo teaches it to watch ring-shaped ones too.

sections.title: The Token Ring Groups
sections.content:
Four groups replace the Ethernet-specific ones: the Mac-Layer Statistics and Promiscuous Statistics groups for current utilization and error counts, and the Mac-Layer History and Promiscuous History groups for the historical versions. The Mac-Layer groups collect error reports and utilization from the MAC layer, while the Promiscuous groups gather utilization from data packets collected promiscuously.

Four more groups are specific to Token Ring. The Ring Station group holds statistics and status for each station on the ring and status for each monitored ring. The Ring Station Order group gives the order of stations on monitored rings. The Ring Station Config group manages stations actively: a station may be removed or have configuration information downloaded from it. The Source Routing group has utilization statistics from the source routing information that packets may carry.

Every group is marked optional to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: Some gauges count traffic and mistakes now and over time. Others list who is on the ring and in what order, and one can even tell a computer to leave the ring.

sections.title: Rules for the Existing RMON Groups
sections.content:
The memo says how the RFC 1271 objects behave on Token Ring. Any MacAddress in this MIB has the source routing bit stripped off, so the address is consistent for every packet a node sends.

In the Host group, only Token Ring isolating errors raise a host entry's error counter: LineErrors, BurstErrors, ACErrors, InternalErrors and AbortErrors, plus congestionErrors. ACErrors count only against the nearest upstream neighbor of the reporting station. LineErrors and BurstErrors count against the reporting station and its upstream neighbor. InternalErrors and AbortErrors count against the reporting station only. In the Matrix group, error counters are never incremented.

For the Filter group, the status bitmask has bit 3 (first packet after some packets were dropped), bit 4 (Frame Copied bit set) and bit 5 (Address Recognized bit set). Filters assume a 32 byte RIF field. The RFC also warns that, because soft error report packets may be sent with assured delivery, some errors may be reported twice on devices that monitor promiscuously.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo sets counting rules, such as which kinds of mistakes get blamed on which computer on the ring.

sections.title: Definitions and Conventions
sections.content:
The module is TOKEN-RING-RMON-MIB, rooted at tokenRing, which is { rmon 10 }. It uses a MacAddress convention of six octets in IEEE 802.1a canonical order, even though 802.5 transmits addresses most significant bit first. TimeInterval is measured in units of 0.01 seconds.

The memo adopts the 802.5 definition of a good frame: bounded by a valid start and end delimiter, a whole number of octets, only 0 and 1 bits, FF bits of the GC field equal to 00 or 01, a valid FCS, and at least 18 octets between the delimiters.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo fixes a few small details, like what counts as a good message and how addresses are written, so every tool reads the gauges the same way.
